Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Silver # Silver ## Recent trends At $11.55/oz, silver successfully challenged its 1987 peak in 2006 and averaged its highest level since 1984 in real terms ($14.08/oz). The fourth quarter of 2006 has also been a record in its own right (and not only when compared with the second quarter of that year), it too breaking the 1987 peaks in real terms. However, silver failed to make a successful challenge on a daily basis, which leaves the high London fix at $14.94/oz in May (this also has the highest monthly average). This said, silver has had quite a strong end to the year. Silver’s peak in May was followed by a severe fall to around $10/oz. September’s peak was more modest than that in May, but October’s trough was higher than that in June. November marked the breaking point of a narrowing trading range in place since May, silver surging to another peak in December before slipping relatively modestly towards $12/oz in early January. - Strong silver prices are justified given that stocks remain equivalent to approximately one year’s consumption. In such an environment, ferocious demand for silver as an investment has exacerbated the fundamentally driven price. The launch of Barclays’ iShares ETF has arguably been the most talked about development in the silver market in 2006. It has accumulated 3,768t of metal. However, we estimate that the market only had a surplus of about 750t last year and so this implies that about 3,000t has simply been transferred from other holdings on a net basis. Indeed, we believe that government-related stocks have fallen by about 2,000t and we know that exchange stocks have fallen by 282t. About 750t most therefore have been withdrawn from other privately held holdings. - Given that the silver market only generated a surplus of 750t in 2006, it is hardly surprising that the accumulation of silver to back an ETF had such a significant impact on the price. After all, it was not sufficient to push the stock ratio significantly higher. The surplus would have been even higher if mine supply growth had not been derailed by Cannington’s cut back. Our provisional estimate of mine supply in 2006 is barely higher than that in 2005. This is not to say, however, that the mining sector’s response to higher prices has been muted. We expect output at Cannington in calendar 2006 to have fallen by around 500t. For overall supplies to be roughly unchanged, the net supply from all other mines must have increased by this much, i.e. 2.5–3.0%. - Fabrication demand disappointed in 2006. Its use in photography has again fallen sharply, and customs data suggest that the demand in jewellery has weakened. Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Silver 73 ### Silver: Demand growth to remain subdued in the short term ###### Demand disappoints in 2006 The sharp erosion of silver's use in the photographic industry w as alw ays going to be a drag on overall silver demand. How ever, demand from the jew ellery sector has also been poor in 2006. Furthermore, the grow th in silver's use by the electrical and electronics industry is also beginning to slow . Silver consumption looks set to fall by 2-3% (600-700t) in 2006. Offtake from the photographic industry is estimated to have fallen by at least 400t, leaving it at just 63% of the level at its peak in 1999. Meanw hile, demand from the jew ellery and silverw are sector could have fallen by 800t. The electrical and electronics sector w as supportive, but its demand lifted by no more than 300t. A combination of further structural erosion of photgraphy use, poor demand in jew ellery, and a slow ing electronics sector, should hold back total silver demand in the short term. ###### World photographic offtake has continued to decline sharply

74 Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Silver ### Silver: Further new projects adding to future mine supply ##### After zero growth in 2006, mine supply is about to accelerate higher Global mine supply should have barely changed in 2006. Of course, mine projects are struggling because of a shortage of labour and equipment (and delays in financing). For this reason, w e have increased our allow ance for disruption for the next few years. Nevertheless, the stage is set for several years of strong grow th. The grow th in 2007 w ill mainly reflect Cannington's return to full production. But w ith San Cristobal ramping up tow ards year-end, grow th w ill accelerate in 2008. A flurry of new projects w ill supply more than an extra 3,000t (this now includes some marginal projects) by 2010. Some arguably less likely projects could also be supplying then, but w e assume that low er prices w ill ultimately derail some of these before they have a chance to supply. Most of the grow th that w e forecast is thus from committed projects. ##### Mine revenues have surged in 2006 350

The impact of 2006’s high prices on miners’ revenues is shown in the _Storyboard_ . A significant amount of new activity was said to have emerged in Mexico, which has traditionally been home to a significant small-scale and informal mining sector. However, we have also been aware of a number of formal, albeit not major, companies pursuing their aims of being silver miners. We have therefore decided to rework all of our Mexican mine supply numbers to ensure that we have a clearer picture of developments in the country. A key area of concern this year has been that some of the recent developments of the formal mining sector operating in Mexico have also been ranked as the implied ballooning of supply from the informal sector. Any estimates and forecast would thus involve double counting. Our rework has certainly indicated that this has occurred. Our estimates of supply in 2005 and 2006 have been lowered as a result. We now doubt that supply in 2005 exceeded 3,000 tonnes and we do not believe that it is close to 3,500 tonnes in 2006. In the case of 2005, we can identify 93% of silver mine supply (little more than 200 tonnes has not been identified). The most important conclusion from the rework has been that the current boom in Mexican mine supply has been underpinned by the formal mining sector. Our data now imply that 78% of the growth in Mexico’s mine supply in 2005 emerged fr

om the formal mining sector (and all in 2006). Whereas informal mining responds swiftly to the rise and fall of metal prices, the response from formal mining is less elastic in the short term. Furthermore, in addition to eliminating a number of cases of probable double counting, our rework has unearthed a huge number of projects, a couple of which are close to being commissioned. Together with recent additions, these have increased our forecast for 2008 by almost 175-200 tonnes and by over 350 t/y thereafter. The large scale of the difference to our previous forecast in these later years stems from the fact that growth in supply is emerging from the formal sector. The “new” silver mining companies involved in many of these developments will not be intending to cut back output or close their operations when prices are low because they have no other revenue streams. Of course, as in previous periods of low prices, similar companies have gone bankrupt and their supplies have ceased. Our forecast shows that committed Mexican mine supply will be more than 850 tonnes higher in 2011 than it was in 2005. Within this, nine companies will be contributing at least an extra 50 tonnes. The single largest addition on a corporate level should be Gammon Lake. Its existing operation was the El Cubo silver-gold mine complex (previously known as Las Torres when under Peсoles’ control), which it acquired when it acquired MexGold Resources. However, it started operating (initially heap leaching) at the Ocampo project early in 2006 and a mill is currently being commissioned. Contributing an extra 180 tonnes, Pan American Silver will more than double its output in Mexico when it brings its recently commissioned Alamo Dorado up to full capacity. Meanwhile, Fresnillo’s expansion will boost Peсoles’ output and Endeavor Silver should ultimately produce in excess of 100 t/y. Three other mines will be commissioned next year. La Parrilla should lift First Majestic’s output by 60 t/y, and Metallica Resources and Minefinders will together add close to 200 t/y. There are a good number of early stage projects being considered and can by no means be considered as committed developments. 76 Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Silver |Committed Me|xican silver mine produ
